a: It was the twelfth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Assyrians
p: The real Nebuchadnezzar ruled Babylon, not Assyria, and Nineveh had fallen before he became king.
b:
Nebuchadnezzar II was king of Babylon from 605 to 562 BC (2 Kings 24:1, "Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon"). He never ruled "the Assyrians," and Nineveh, Assyria's capital, was destroyed in 612 BC by his father Nabopolassar and the Medes, seven years before his reign began. To a Jewish reader the first line is as jarring as "Napoleon, king of the Germans, in Moscow" would be to us.

Three answers are given. Most scholars think the clash is deliberate: the author fuses Israel's two great destroyers, Assyria and Babylon, into one enemy and signals that this is a story, not a chronicle. Older Catholic defenders of the book's history held that the name stands for another king: F. Vigouroux proposed Ashurbanipal of Assyria (668–627 BC), whose officers took King Manasseh captive (2 Chronicles 33:11), while A. Calmet kept the real Nebuchadnezzar and blamed copyists for other names. On the Catholic answer from literary genre, see the chapter page.
r: 2 Kings 24:1; 2 Kings 25:8–9; 2 Chronicles 33:11; Daniel 1:1; Nahum 3:7; Zephaniah 2:13

a: Nineveh, the great city
p: The same title Genesis and Jonah give Nineveh.
b: Genesis lists Nineveh among the cities Nimrod's people built, "that is the great city" (Genesis 10:11–12), and Jonah calls it "the great city" four times (Jonah 1:2; 3:2–3; 4:11). Jonah's Nineveh repented in sackcloth, even its cattle (Jonah 3:7–8). In Judith the roles are turned around: Nineveh sends the army, and Israel puts on sackcloth, cattle and all (4:10).

a: In those days Arphaxad ruled over the Medes in Ecbatana
t: Arphaxad, the king no list knows
p: No Median king was named Arphaxad. The name is the Greek form of Arpachshad, a son of Shem.
b:
Arphaxad is the Septuagint spelling of Arpachshad, Shem's son (Genesis 10:22, "Shem's sons were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud and Aram"; Luke 3:36). No Median king had that name. Herodotus names the Median kings Deioces, who founded Ecbatana, then Phraortes, Cyaxares and Astyages (Histories 1.96–130).

A. Calmet, as the Catholic Encyclopedia reports him, identified Arphaxad with Phraortes, while keeping the real Nebuchadnezzar (F. Vigouroux later paired Phraortes with Ashurbanipal, his contemporary), who, Herodotus says, died making war on the Assyrians (Histories 1.102); others proposed Deioces, the builder of Ecbatana's walls (1:2–4). Most scholars think the author chose an old biblical name for a fictional rival king, as he chose Nebuchadnezzar for the villain. The Medes of the story are the Medes of the 600s and 500s BC, the age when Media and Babylon really did fight over Assyria's ruins.

a: Around Ecbatana he built walls
p: From its first verses Judith's Greek is full of Hebrew word order and idioms. Many think it was translated from Hebrew.
b: Almost every clause of Judith begins with "and" (kai, Hebrew ve-), verbs come first, and Hebrew idioms are put into Greek word for word: "a month of days" (3:10), "very, very" (4:2), "they humbled their souls" (4:9), "do not let your face fall" (6:9). Most scholars (Moore; Enslin) think the book was written in Hebrew and that the Greek is a close translation. Jerome says he translated from a "Chaldean" (Aramaic) copy, and Origen learned from Jewish teachers that they had no Hebrew Judith in his day. A minority, notably Jan Joosten, hold that it was written in Greek by an author imitating the Septuagint's biblical style. The Plain smooths these idioms into English and flags the important ones in notes.
orig: καὶ ᾠκοδόμησεν ἐπ᾽ Ἐκβατάνων (kai ōkodomēsen ep' Ekbatanōn), 'and he built upon Ecbatana'

a: He made the wall seventy cubits high and fifty cubits thick
p: Seventy cubits is about 105 feet. The towers (1:3) would be about 150 feet tall.
b: A cubit was about a foot and a half. Ecbatana (modern Hamadan in western Iran) was the Median capital, and Herodotus describes its seven circles of walls, each painted a different color (Histories 1.98). But walls 105 feet high and 75 feet thick, with 150-foot towers, are beyond any ancient city. The storyteller makes Arphaxad's fortress as strong as words can make it, so that Nebuchadnezzar's capture of it (1:14) shows a power no city can stop, until it meets Bethulia.

a: in the territory of Ragau
p: Ragau is the Median city Rages (Rhagae), near modern Tehran, the city of Tobit's silver.
b: Rages (modern Rey, on the southern edge of Tehran) lay at the foot of the Elburz mountains, which explains "the mountains of Ragau" (1:15). It is the town where Tobit left his silver with Gabael (Tobit 1:14; Tobit 5:6). Both books treat Media as the far east of the Jewish world.

a: All who lived in the hill country came to meet him
p: The Greek says only "to him". It may mean Nebuchadnezzar or Arphaxad.
b: The verb synēntēsan pros auton can mean "came to meet him" as allies or "came against him" in battle. Since the western nations refuse to help Nebuchadnezzar (1:11), many readers take these eastern peoples as his allies; others think they gathered to Arphaxad. Sinaiticus as first written says these peoples came "to war" (eis polemon), and its corrector reads "came to meet him in war" (Swete's apparatus: προς αυτον] εις πολεμον ℵ* προς αυτον εις πολ. ℵc.a), which favors the reading that they fought against him, on Arphaxad's side. The Plain keeps the Greek's "him."

a: the Hydaspes
p: The Hydaspes is a river in the Punjab, where Alexander the Great fought in 326 BC.
b: The Euphrates and Tigris are Mesopotamia's rivers, but the Hydaspes (the Jhelum) is far east in India, famous to Greek readers for Alexander's battle against King Porus. Its name here suggests an author who knew Greek geography, though some think it is a slip for the Choaspes, the river of Susa. "Arioch" is a king's name in Genesis 14:1, and "the Elymeans" are the people of Elymais, the Greek name for Elam, where Antiochus IV tried to rob a temple (1 Maccabees 6:1–4).

a: Persia
p: Persia did not become a power until Cyrus, about 550 BC, after Nebuchadnezzar's death.
b: Under the real Nebuchadnezzar, Persia was a small kingdom under Median rule. The book's map is the map of the Persian and Greek centuries: Persia, Cilicia, Lebanon and Antilebanon, the coast, Egypt. Like the Persian names Holofernes and Bagoas (see 2:4), it is one of the signs that the story was written long after the time it describes.

a: the great plain of Esdraelon
p: Esdraelon is the Greek name of the Jezreel Valley, the wide plain below the hills of Samaria.
b: Judith's Greek spells it four ways: Esrēm here, Esdraēlōn (3:9), Esrēlōn (4:6) and Esdrēlōn (7:3). All are forms of Hebrew Yizre'el, Jezreel. The plain was the natural highway for armies entering the land from the north, where Gideon fought Midian (Judges 6:33) and Saul fell (1 Samuel 29:1; 1 Samuel 31:1). The Plain uses "Esdraelon" throughout, the name English Bibles use for Judith and later history.

a: Tahpanhes and Rameses and all the land of Goshen
p: These are names from Israel's history in Egypt: Goshen, Rameses and Tahpanhes.
b: Goshen is where Jacob's family settled (Genesis 47:4, "let your servants live in the land of Goshen"), Rameses is a store city the Israelites built (Exodus 1:11), and Tahpanhes is where Jeremiah was taken (Jeremiah 43:7). The "river of Egypt" is the wadi on Egypt's border (Numbers 34:5, "the Wadi of Egypt"). Betane and Chelous are unknown; Kadesh is probably Kadesh-barnea. The list runs down the coast road from Syria into Egypt, the route every invader took.

a: Tanis and Memphis
p: Tanis is the Bible's Zoan, in the Nile Delta; Memphis was Lower Egypt's ancient capital.
b: Zoan (Tanis) appears in Numbers 13:22 and in Psalm 78:12, "in the land of Egypt, in the open country of Zoan." Memphis is the Bible's Noph (Isaiah 19:13; Jeremiah 46:14). "Ethiopia" is Cush, the land south of Egypt, the end of the known world in that direction.

a: He swore by his throne and his kingdom
t: A king who swears by himself
p: In the Bible only God swears by himself. Nebuchadnezzar swears by his own throne.
b: When God makes an oath there is no one greater to swear by, so he swears by himself (Genesis 22:16, "By myself I swear, says the LORD"; Isaiah 45:23; Hebrews 6:13). Nebuchadnezzar swears by his throne and kingdom, and he will soon say "as I live" (2:12), the oath only God takes in the Bible. The book is setting up its question: who is god, the king or the God of Israel (3:8; 6:2)?

a: the two seas
p: Probably the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the edges of Egypt and Syria.
b: The phrase is unexplained. Most take it as the Mediterranean on the west and the Red Sea (or the Persian Gulf) on the south and east, so that the king's oath takes in everything from Cilicia to Egypt. Notice that the oath names Moab, Ammon and Idumea, the peoples who will join his army (5:2; 7:8), but in Vaticanus it does not name Judea; see the variant.

a: turned its beauty into its shame
p: A Hebrew turn of phrase: the city's glory becomes its disgrace.
b: The Greek ton kosmon autēs ethēken eis oneidos autēs, "he put its ornament into its reproach," reads like Hebrew. The prophets use the same reversal of honor and shame (Hosea 4:7, where God will change their glory into disgrace). The word kosmos, "ornament, beauty," will return when Judith adorns herself to go out against Holofernes (10:4).

a: ran him through with his hunting spears
p: The Greek sibynē is a light spear for hunting. Arphaxad is killed like game in the hills.
b: A sibynē was a light hunting spear or javelin. The picture is of a king run down in the mountains like an animal. The clause "he destroyed him once and for all that day" renders a Greek "until that day" (heōs tēs hēmeras ekeinēs), probably a Hebrew idiom ("to this day") put into Greek a little awkwardly; Sinaiticus reads "this day."
orig: κατηκόντισεν αὐτὸν ἐν ταῖς σιβύναις (katēkontisen auton en tais sibynais)

a: for a hundred and twenty days
p: Like Ahasuerus in Esther, the conqueror celebrates for months. Meanwhile his anger at the west waits.
b: Persian kings were famous for long feasts: Ahasuerus showed off his wealth "for many days: 180 days in all" (Esther 1:4). The pause also builds tension: the king's oath of revenge (1:12) hangs over the west through the whole feast, and the campaign begins only in the next year (2:1).

a: In the eighteenth year
p: In the real Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year (587/586 BC) Jerusalem fell.
b: Jeremiah dates the deportation from Jerusalem to "the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar" (Jeremiah 52:29), and Kings dates the burning of the temple to his nineteenth (2 Kings 25:8–9, "the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar"). Many scholars think the date was chosen on purpose: the story opens in the year that Israel remembered as the end of everything, and this time the temple does not fall. The Vulgate reads "the thirteenth year" (see the variant).

a: there was talk in the palace
t: A word that came to the king's house
p: The Greek "a word came about" is the formula the Septuagint uses when God's word comes to a prophet.
b: The phrase egeneto logos, "a word came to be," is how the Greek Old Testament says "the word of the LORD came to" a prophet (for example Jeremiah 1:4 and Jonah 1:1 in the Septuagint). Here the word comes from the king's own house. Much of Judith is a contest of words: Nebuchadnezzar's "I have spoken, and I will do" (2:12), Holofernes' "not one of my words will fail" (6:9), and finally the God whose word does stand.
orig: ἐγένετο λόγος ἐν οἴκῳ (egeneto logos en oikō)

a: his secret plan
p: The Greek mystērion is the word Daniel's Greek uses for the secret God reveals.
b: Nebuchadnezzar "set before them the mystērion of his counsel." In the Greek of Daniel 2 the same word stands for the Aramaic raz, the secret of the king's dream that only God can reveal (Daniel 2:18–19, 27–30). In Judith the king's secret is a plan to destroy. The next clause, literally "he completed all the evil of the earth from his mouth," is obscure. The Plain takes it to mean he spelled out the harm he planned for the earth; others read "the evil of the earth" as the land's wickedness, its disobedience to him, which he recounted to his council (compare 2:3; 2:6).
orig: τὸ μυστήριον τῆς βουλῆς αὐτοῦ (to mystērion tēs boulēs autou)

a: all flesh
p: A Hebrew way of saying "every living person". The king plans a flood of destruction.
b: Hebrew kol basar, "all flesh," means every living being. It is the phrase of the Flood story: "The end of all flesh is coming before me" (Genesis 6:13). The echo is pointed. In Genesis it is God who decides to destroy all flesh; here a king takes God's place.

a: Holofernes
p: Holofernes is a Persian name, and a Holophernes really served a Persian king in the 300s BC.
b:
The name is the Greek form of the Old Persian Orophernes. Diodorus of Sicily tells of a Holophernes, brother of the king of Cappadocia, who fought for the Persian king Artaxerxes III in his campaign against Egypt (343 BC; Diodorus 31.19); in the same campaign a eunuch named Bagoas was the king's most trusted officer (Diodorus 16.47). Judith also has a eunuch Bagoas (12:11). Another Orophernes briefly held the throne of Cappadocia about 158 BC with Seleucid support, within the first readers' memory.

Y. M. Grintz argued from this that the story grew out of the Persian period. Most scholars think the author borrowed famous Persian names, as he borrowed Nebuchadnezzar's, to build a composite villain. "Second only to himself" recalls Joseph (Genesis 41:40, "Only on the throne will I be greater than you") and Haman.

a: the commander in chief
p: The Greek archistratēgos is the highest army rank. Joshua's heavenly visitor bears the same title.
b: In the Septuagint archistratēgos is used for the "commander of the LORD's army" who meets Joshua (Joshua 5:14) and for generals like Sisera (Judges 4:2) and Abner. Holofernes is Nebuchadnezzar's second in command. The Plain renders the title "commander in chief" throughout the book.

a: the great king, the lord of the whole earth
t: "The great king, the lord of the whole earth"
p: The first title was used by Assyrian and Persian kings. The second belongs to God.
b: "The great king" is how the Rabshakeh introduces Sennacherib at the walls of Jerusalem: "The great king, the king of Assyria, says this" (2 Kings 18:19), and Persian kings called themselves "the great king, king of kings." But "the Lord of all the earth" is God's title, as in "the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth" (Joshua 3:11; Micah 4:13; Zechariah 4:14). Nebuchadnezzar opens with a prophet's formula, "This is what … says," and claims God's own title.

a: Tell them to get earth and water ready
p: The Persian kings demanded "earth and water" as a token that a people surrendered.
b: Herodotus tells how Darius and Xerxes sent heralds to the Greek cities asking for "earth and water," the symbols of handing over the land (Histories 6.48; 7.32; 7.131–133). The custom is Persian, not Babylonian. It is one of the clearest signs that the author pictured his "Assyrian" empire with Persian colors.

a: to my troops
p: The Greek says only "I will give them to them as plunder." The Plain supplies "my troops."
b: Literally, "I will give them for plunder to them" (dōsō autous eis diarpagēn autois). The second "them" has nothing to refer back to; it most likely means the king's soldiers, whose feet have just covered the earth. The Plain says so to make the sentence readable.
orig: δώσω αὐτοὺς εἰς διαρπαγὴν αὐτοῖς (dōsō autous eis diarpagēn autois)

a: Their slain
p: The Greek word usually means "wounded", but here, as often in the Septuagint, it stands for Hebrew "slain".
b: Greek traumatiai means "wounded men." The Septuagint uses it to translate Hebrew chalalim, "the slain," people pierced to death in battle, and that is the sense here: the ravines are filled with the dead. The same word returns in 6:6, where Achior is told he will fall "among their slain." It is one more sign of a Hebrew original behind the Greek.

a: do not let your eye spare them
p: A Hebrew idiom for showing no pity. The king borrows the language of Israel's holy war.
b: Hebrew lo' tachos 'enekha, "your eye shall not spare," is the wording of Deuteronomy's commands about the Canaanites, which the site's Plain gives as "Do not look on them with pity" (Deuteronomy 7:16; compare Deuteronomy 13:8; Ezekiel 9:5). Nebuchadnezzar gives his general the orders that the Torah gives Israel. The last words, literally "in all your land," must mean the lands Holofernes will rule for the king.
orig: οὐ φείσεται ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου (ou pheisetai ho ophthalmos sou)

a: as I live
p: In the Bible this is the oath of the living God. Here a king takes it on his own lips.
b: "As I live, declares the LORD" is God's oath (Numbers 14:28; Deuteronomy 32:40; Ezekiel 33:11). Kings and people swear "as the LORD lives." Nebuchadnezzar swears by his own life and power, and he ends, "I have spoken, and I will do," words that echo God's "Would he say a thing and not do it?" (Numbers 23:19). The book's first readers would hear blasphemy in every line.

a: Carry them out to the full
p: A Hebrew way of stressing a verb by doubling it, put word for word into Greek.
b: The Greek epitelōn epiteleseis, "completing you shall complete," copies the Hebrew infinitive absolute, which repeats a verb for emphasis (as in Genesis 2:17, "dying you shall die"). The Plain renders the sense: carry them out to the full.

a: a hundred and twenty thousand, and twelve thousand mounted archers
p: The army numbers 132,000 here and grows to 182,000 at Bethulia (7:2).
b: Ancient armies of more than a hundred thousand were rare and could not have been supplied on the march described here. The figures belong to the story's scale, like the huge walls of Ecbatana (1:2–4). The point is the contrast: the greatest army on earth against one hill town, and, in the end, one widow.

a: like locusts, like the sand of the earth
p: The words recall Gideon's enemies, Midian and the peoples of the East.
b: Judges says of Midian, "Midian, Amalek and all the people of the East were sprawled over the valley like a swarm of locusts. Their camels were past counting, as many as the grains of sand on the shore of the sea" (Judges 7:12; compare Judges 6:5). Holofernes will soon burn the Midianites' own tents (2:26). Readers who knew Judges knew that such hordes fell to a small band, and to a woman with a tent peg (Judges 4:21).

a: three days' journey
p: Bectileth near Cilicia is about 300 miles from Nineveh, not three days. The route that follows zigzags across the map.
b:
From Nineveh the army reaches Cilicia, in southeastern Turkey, in three days, then goes to Put and Lud, back across the Euphrates into Mesopotamia, back to Cilicia, south to Midian in Arabia, and north again to Damascus (2:21–27). No real campaign could follow this route.

Critical scholars read the geography as part of the book's deliberate fantasy, or as the work of an author who knew Judea well and the east only by name. Defenders of the book's history have blamed copyists for garbled names, and some places (Bectileth, the wadi Abron) cannot now be identified at all. "To the north" renders "on the left," the Hebrew way of giving directions while facing east (see Tobit 1:2).

a: Put and Lud
t: Names from the table of nations
p: Put and Lud are peoples listed in Genesis 10, usually placed in Africa and Asia Minor.
b: Put is a son of Ham (Genesis 10:6, "Ham's sons were Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan"), usually located in Libya; Lud is a son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), often taken as Lydia in Asia Minor. Ezekiel names them as hired soldiers (Ezekiel 27:10; Ezekiel 30:5). "Rassis" is unknown. The Ishmaelites are the Arab tribes of the desert (Genesis 25:12–18).

a: He came to the borders of Japheth
t: Claude's theory: Holofernes conquers the map of Genesis 10
p: Claude's idea: the campaign is drawn on the map of Noah's sons, so that Holofernes conquers "the whole earth".
b: This is my own suggestion. "Japheth" is not a known country; it is the name of Noah's son, whose descendants fill the north and west in Genesis 10:2–5. With Put and Lud (2:23), the Ishmaelites and Midian, the campaign takes in the families of Shem, Ham and Japheth, the whole human race as Genesis maps it. That fits the king's claim to be "lord of the whole earth" (2:5) and to destroy "all flesh" (2:3), the language of the Flood. Commentators have noted the table-of-nations names; reading the whole route as a deliberate conquest of Genesis 10 is my own synthesis.

a: winnowed their plains bare
p: A harvest picture: as a farmer tosses grain to the wind, Holofernes scatters the people of the plain.
b: The verb exelikmēsen means "winnowed," tossing threshed grain so the wind blows the chaff away. It is harvest time (wheat ripens in May and June), and Holofernes burns the crops and "winnows" the people. The prophets use the same image for judgment (Jeremiah 15:7; Isaiah 41:16). "The edge of the sword" is literally "the mouth of the sword," a Hebrew idiom.

a: Jamnia
p: Jamnia, Ashdod and Ashkelon were cities the Maccabees fought over in the 160s–140s BC.
b: Jamnia is Hebrew Jabneh (Yavneh); Ashdod is Greek Azotus. Judas Maccabeus fought near both (1 Maccabees 4:15; 1 Maccabees 5:58; 2 Maccabees 12:8–9), and his brother Jonathan burned the temple of Dagon at Azotus (1 Maccabees 10:84). For Judith's first readers the coastal plain was a real and recent frontier. "Sur" and "Ocina" are uncertain; some identify Ocina with Akko (Ptolemais).

a: lie before you
p: The envoys "lie before" Holofernes: they lie face down, and they lie open to whatever he does.
b: The Greek parakeimetha enōpion sou, "we lie beside, before you," is used again in 3:3 of their fields and flocks, which "lie before" him too. The people and their goods are equally at his disposal. "As seems good in your eyes" (3:4) and "as is pleasing to your face" (3:2, literally) are Hebrew idioms for "as you like."

a: Come and deal with them as seems good in your eyes
t: The surrender Bethulia will be tempted to make
p: The coastal cities say what the thirsty people of Bethulia will beg their rulers to say (7:26–27).
b: The coast's words of total surrender are the model the townspeople of Bethulia will later demand: "hand the whole town over to be plundered … We will be slaves, but we will stay alive" (7:26–27). Surrender does not save the coast: Holofernes still destroys their gods and their groves (3:8). The reader learns early that Nebuchadnezzar's mercy is no mercy.

a: garlands, dancing and tambourines
p: Garlands, dancing and tambourines were how Israel celebrated God's victories.
b: Miriam and the women go out "with hand drums and with dancing" after the Sea (Exodus 15:20), and the women greet David with dancing and drums (1 Samuel 18:6). Here the cities give that welcome to the invader. At the end of the book Israel's women will dance in Judith's honor, and she and her companions, crowned with olive leaves, will lead the dance (15:12–13).

a: Yet he laid waste all their territory and cut down their sacred groves
p: The Greek says "all their borders". Many scholars think it once read "all their shrines".
b: Vaticanus has horia, "borders, territory." Two Greek words that look alike, horia and hiera ("shrines"), are confused elsewhere in the book (at 4:1 Alexandrinus reads horia where Vaticanus has hiera), and the next clause is about destroying the gods, so many scholars think the original said Holofernes demolished their shrines. The Plain keeps the manuscript. "Sacred groves" (alsē) are the Asherah poles that the Torah told Israel to cut down (Deuteronomy 7:5, "chop down their Asherah poles"): Holofernes does what Israel's law commanded, but in order to make the nations worship a man.
orig: κατέσκαψεν πάντα τὰ ὅρια αὐτῶν (kateskapsen panta ta horia autōn)

a: every language and tribe would call on him as god
p: Daniel 3 and the crisis under Antiochus IV both turn on a king who demands worship.
b:
Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue, before which "all the peoples, nations and languages" must bow (Daniel 3:4–7), is the closest parallel in the 66 books. The first readers had a nearer one: Antiochus IV called himself Epiphanes, "god made manifest," ordered all peoples in his kingdom to give up their own customs (1 Maccabees 1:41–50), and set up an altar to Zeus in the temple in 167 BC. Daniel describes such a king who "will exalt himself above every god" (Daniel 11:36).

This is the book's central question, asked aloud in 6:2: "Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" Judith's prayer gives Israel's answer (9:14).

a: the great ridge of Judea
p: The Greek word means "saw", probably a saw-toothed ridge of hills.
b: The Greek prion is a saw. It probably describes a jagged ridge, perhaps the line of hills south of the Jezreel Valley, the northern edge of the hill country that leads to Judea, or the Carmel range. The KJV, following other texts, has "the great strait of Judea." Dothan, a town on the main road south from the valley, is where Joseph found his brothers (Genesis 37:17) and where an Aramean army surrounded Elisha (2 Kings 6:13).
orig: τοῦ πρίονος τοῦ μεγάλου τῆς Ἰουδαίας (tou prionos tou megalou tēs Ioudaias)

a: Scythopolis
p: Scythopolis, "city of the Scythians", was the Greek name of Beth-shean, used from the 200s BC.
b: Beth-shean, at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley, is where the Philistines hung Saul's body (1 Samuel 31:10). The Greek name Scythopolis is first attested in the Hellenistic period, centuries after Nebuchadnezzar; 2 Maccabees 12:29–31 uses it in the story of Judas Maccabeus. Geba here is not Benjamin's Geba but an unknown place nearby.

a: a whole month
p: The Greek copies a Hebrew phrase, "a month of days", meaning a full month.
b: The same Hebrew idiom stands in Genesis 29:14, where Jacob "stayed with him a full month" (literally "a month of days"). Holofernes uses the month to gather his supplies, and Judea uses it to get ready (4:1–8).

a: The Israelites who lived in Judea
p: In Judith, "Israel" lives in Judea, with Jerusalem's temple at its center and no king.
b: The book calls the people "the Israelites" (literally "the sons of Israel") and "Israel," but they live in "Judea," the Greek name for the small temple province of the Persian and Greek periods. There is no king of Judah anywhere in the story; the high priest and a council of elders govern (4:6–8). That is the shape of Jewish life after the exile, from Ezra and Nehemiah to the Hasmoneans. Holofernes will ask "Who has risen up over them as king?" (5:3), and the answer the book gives is: none but God.

a: They were very, very afraid of him
p: The Greek doubles "very", copying the Hebrew me'od me'od.
b: Greek sphodra sphodra is Hebrew me'od me'od put word for word (as in Genesis 7:19, "very, very"). The fear is for "the temple of the Lord their God," not only for their lives. The Plain keeps the doubled word.

a: For they had only lately come up from captivity
t: Back from an exile that had not happened yet
p: If Nebuchadnezzar is king, the exile is still in the future. Yet the Jews are "lately" back and the temple newly cleansed.
b:
Nebuchadnezzar took Judah into exile (2 Kings 24–25), and Jews came back only after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC (Ezra 1:1–4). Judith puts the return, and a temple "made holy again after they were defiled," inside Nebuchadnezzar's reign. Achior repeats it (5:18–19).

Critical view. The author sets the story in a timeless after-the-exile Israel. The cleansing of a defiled temple would make the first readers think of 164 BC, when Judas Maccabeus purified the temple that Antiochus had profaned (1 Maccabees 4:36–59), the feast of Hanukkah.

Older Catholic defenders. Vigouroux, as the Catholic Encyclopedia reports him, placed the story under Manasseh, who was taken to Babylon by Assyria's officers, "brought him back to Jerusalem," and then "removed the foreign gods … from the LORD's house" (2 Chronicles 33:11–15). Others dated it after Ezra, under the Persian kings.

Catholic teaching today lets the question of genre decide (see the chapter page).

a: the vessels, the altar and the house had been made holy again after they were defiled
p: Twice in Israel's memory a defiled temple was cleansed and rededicated: after the exile, and in 164 BC.
b: After the return, "the Israelites, the priests, the Levites and the rest of the people of the exile joyfully held the dedication of this house of God" (Ezra 6:16). Hezekiah also cleansed the temple and its vessels after Ahaz (2 Chronicles 29:15–19). But "defilement" (bebēlōsis) of the altar and the vessels points most clearly to Antiochus IV, who took the temple's vessels and set up "the abomination of desolation" on the altar (1 Maccabees 1:21–23; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:42–51; Daniel 11:31).
r: Ezra 6:16; 2 Chronicles 29:15–19; 1 Maccabees 1:21–23; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:42–51; Daniel 11:31

a: every district of Samaria
p: After the exile Samaria was a separate province. Judith counts it as Israel's land.
b: In Ezra and Nehemiah the people of Samaria are rivals of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:1–24; Nehemiah 4:1–2). In the 100s BC the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus conquered Samaria and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254–256; 13.275–281). A book that sends Jerusalem's orders to "every district of Samaria" and sets its heroine in a Samarian hill town reflects either that conquest or the hope behind it. Kona is unknown (the KJV reads "the villages"); Beth-horon guards the western road up to Jerusalem, where the Maccabees won battles (1 Maccabees 3:16–24; 1 Maccabees 7:39–43).

a: their fields had just been harvested
p: The story takes place in early summer, just after the grain harvest, so the towns had food stored.
b: Wheat was harvested in May and June (Holofernes burned Damascus's wheat fields, 2:27), and Judith's husband died of sunstroke during the barley harvest (8:2–3). Fresh grain meant the hill towns could stock up. Water, not food, will be their weakness (7:12–13).

a: Joakim, the high priest who was then in Jerusalem
p: A Joiakim was high priest after the exile (Nehemiah 12:10). In Judith he leads the nation like a ruler.
b:
Nehemiah lists "Joiakim son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak" as high priest after the return (Nehemiah 12:10; Nehemiah 12:26), about 500 BC. Some defenders of the book's history have pointed to him, and the Catholic Encyclopedia article dated Judith's events by this Joakim. Baruch 1:7 names another Joakim. The Vulgate calls him Eliachim (4:5 and 4:11 in its numbering), which is another form of the name (compare 2 Kings 23:34).

More important is his role. He writes orders to the towns, commands the defense and leads worship (4:14; 15:8). In the 140s BC the Hasmonean Simon was made "high priest, general and ruler" of the nation (1 Maccabees 14:41–47). Judith's first readers would see their own government in Joakim.

a: Bethulia
p: No town called Bethulia is known outside Judith. Its name may be a symbol.
b:
The story places Bethulia on a hill near Dothan, above springs, facing the Jezreel Valley, guarding the pass to Jerusalem (4:6–7; 6:11; 7:3). No ancient source outside the book names it, and no site fits every detail. Proposals include Mithilia (C. R. Conder, favored in the Catholic Encyclopedia), Sanur and other hills near Dothan, and Shechem itself (C. C. Torrey), whose springs, mountains and Simeonite story (Genesis 34; 9:2) fit the plot.

The name has been read as Hebrew betulah, "virgin," or as "house of God" (bet-el, Bethel). Those who read the book as a parable take Bethulia as a figure of Israel or Jerusalem, the "virgin daughter of Zion" (Isaiah 37:22) whom the enemy cannot take. Betomasthaim is equally unknown.

a: room for two men at most
p: The narrow pass that two men could hold belongs to the story's drama more than to the map.
b: The approaches from the Jezreel Valley into the hill country are valleys, not a single ledge. A pass so narrow that two men can block it recalls the famous Greek stand at Thermopylae (Herodotus, Histories 7.176). The idea will matter: Holofernes' allies advise him not to attack such heights at all, but to take the water (7:10–13).

a: the council of elders of all the people of Israel, who sat in Jerusalem
p: The Greek gerousia was the governing council of Jerusalem in the Greek period.
b: A gerousia, "council of elders" (from gerōn, "old man"), governed Jerusalem with the high priest under Greek rule. Antiochus III's letter of about 200 BC grants privileges to "the council of elders, the priests and the scribes of the temple" (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–144), and Jonathan writes to Sparta in the name of "the council of elders" (1 Maccabees 12:6). The Plain renders gerousia "the council of elders" throughout Judith (also 11:14; 15:8). It is an institution of the first readers' own day.

a: they humbled themselves
p: This is the Bible's phrase for fasting: "humble yourselves" on the Day of Atonement.
b: Greek etapeinousan tas psychas autōn, "they humbled their souls," is Hebrew 'innah nefesh, the phrase Leviticus uses for the fast of the Day of Atonement: "you are to humble yourselves and do no work at all" (Leviticus 16:29; compare Psalm 35:13; Isaiah 58:3–5). Here it describes a national fast in an emergency, and 4:13 says so plainly: "the people fasted for many days." On whether Christians should keep set fasts, see the card on chapter 8.
orig: ἐταπεινοῦσαν τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν (etapeinousan tas psychas autōn)

a: their cattle
p: Only Judith and Jonah put animals in sackcloth. In Jonah it was the Ninevites who did it.
b: When Jonah preached, the king of Nineveh ordered that "man and beast, herd and flock" fast and be covered with sackcloth (Jonah 3:7–8). Judith turns the scene around: the army comes from Nineveh, and Israel repents in Nineveh's way. The whole household joins: wives, children, resident foreigners, hired workers and slaves, as the whole household kept the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10). In Israel, sackcloth was a coarse cloth of goat hair worn in mourning.

a: lay face down in front of the temple
p: The scene is very close to the Maccabees' prayer before battle in 2 Maccabees 10.
b: Joel calls the priests to wail "between the porch and the altar" in sackcloth (Joel 1:13; 2:17), and Jehoshaphat's Judah stood before the temple when a great army came (2 Chronicles 20:3–13). Closest of all is 2 Maccabees 10:25–26, where Judas Maccabeus' men sprinkle earth on their heads, put sackcloth around their waists and fall down at the foot of the altar before a battle. The first readers knew this kind of prayer from their own wars.

a: They wrapped the altar in sackcloth
p: Even the altar wears sackcloth, a detail the Vulgate keeps too (4:9 in its numbering).
b: No book of the Hebrew Bible dresses the altar in sackcloth. It is as if the altar itself joins the fast and mourns. The things the people beg God to spare are the very things Holofernes was ordered to take: children, wives, towns and the holy place (2:7–11). "The towns of their inheritance" is the land as God's gift to the tribes (Joshua 13–21).

a: the holy place defiled and mocked, for the nations to gloat over
t: The fear of a defiled sanctuary
p: The prayer fears exactly what happened under Antiochus IV in 167 BC.
b: "Holy things" (ta hagia) means the sanctuary. Psalm 79 laments the nations who "have made your holy temple unclean" (Psalm 79:1), and 1 Maccabees 1 tells how Antiochus robbed the temple and set an altar to Zeus on God's altar (1 Maccabees 1:20–24; 1 Maccabees 1:54). "For the nations to gloat over" recalls the prayer of Joel 2:17: do not let your inheritance become a reproach among the nations.

a: The Lord heard their cry and saw their distress
p: The narrator tells us at once that God has heard. The people inside the story will not know it for a long time.
b: The words recall the exodus: "I have seen, yes seen, the suffering of my people who are in Egypt. I have heard their outcry" (Exodus 3:7; compare Exodus 2:24). From here on the reader knows something the people of Bethulia do not. When they are dying of thirst (7:22) and Uzziah sets a five-day limit (7:30), the reader already knows God has answered; the question is only how.

a: the Lord Almighty
p: Greek Kyrios Pantokratōr is how the Septuagint often renders "the LORD of Armies".
b: Greek Pantokratōr, "ruler of all," is the Septuagint's common rendering of Hebrew tseva'ot in the name YHWH tseva'ot, which this site renders "the LORD of Armies," and also of Shaddai in Job. Revelation uses it often ("the Lord God Almighty," Revelation 4:8). In Judith it is Israel's answer to Nebuchadnezzar's claim to be "lord of the whole earth" (2:5). The Plain renders it "the Lord Almighty" throughout the book, and Kyrios alone as "the Lord," since the Greek has no divine name.

a: the regular burnt offering
p: The tamid, the lamb offered every morning and evening, was the heartbeat of temple worship.
b: The Torah orders "two flawless male lambs in their first year, day by day, as a regular burnt offering" (Numbers 28:3; Exodus 29:38–42). Its stopping was the worst sign of the crisis under Antiochus IV (Daniel 8:11; Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:45). Here the priests keep it going in sackcloth: worship does not stop under threat. "The vows" (Greek euchai, which can also mean "prayers") are probably vow offerings, paired with freewill offerings as in Deuteronomy 12:6, "your vow offerings and your freewill offerings."
r: Numbers 28:3; Exodus 29:38–42; Daniel 8:11; Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:45; Deuteronomy 12:6

a: There were ashes on their turbans
p: Priests normally had to keep their heads and clothes clean of mourning signs. Here even they put on ashes.
b: The high priest was forbidden to show mourning (Leviticus 21:10), and priests wore a linen turban as part of their holy dress (Exodus 28:39–40). Putting ashes on the turban shows how desperate the hour is. The Greek word kidaris is used for the priest's headdress. "To look on … for good" is a Hebrew phrase for God's favorable attention, like Nehemiah's "My God, remember me for good" (Nehemiah 5:19).

a: all the rulers of Moab, the generals of Ammon
p: Moab, Ammon and Edom were Israel's enemies in the Bible and in the Maccabean wars.
b: Moab and Ammon were Lot's descendants (Genesis 19:37–38) and Israel's neighbors across the Jordan; the Torah barred them from Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3). Judas Maccabeus fought the Ammonites and the Idumeans, the descendants of Esau (1 Maccabees 5:3–8). In Judith they are Holofernes' guides and advisers (5:2–3; 7:8–18). "Satraps" is the Persian title for provincial governors (Esther 3:12), another Persian touch.

a: you sons of Canaan
p: Holofernes lumps Moab, Ammon and the coast together as Canaanites. In the Bible they are not.
b: Genesis traces Canaan to Ham (Genesis 10:6, 15–19) and Moab and Ammon to Lot (Genesis 19:37–38, "He is the ancestor of the Ammonites to this day"). The foreign general does not know or care about the peoples he rules. The phrase may also be the author's jab: these neighbors are "Canaanites," the peoples Israel drove out (5:16).

a: Who has risen up over them as king, to lead their army
p: Holofernes assumes every people has a king. Israel in Judith has none but God.
b: The question gets no answer from Achior, because there is no king. In the Bible, God is Israel's true king: Gideon refused a crown because "The LORD will rule over you" (Judges 8:23), and God told Samuel that asking for a king meant "so that I am not king over them" (1 Samuel 8:7). The book's leaders are a high priest, elders and, in the end, a widow.

a: Achior, the leader of all the Ammonites
p: A Gentile officer tells Israel's story truly, is thrown out for it, and in the end joins Israel (14:10).
b:
Achior's name may mean "brother of light" (Hebrew 'achi-'or). He is an Ammonite, a people the Torah barred from Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), yet he speaks the truth about Israel's God before the enemy and suffers for it. In 14:10 he is circumcised and joins the house of Israel.

Readers have compared him with Balaam, the foreign prophet who could only bless Israel (Numbers 22–24), and with Rahab, the Canaanite who confessed Israel's God (Joshua 2:9–11). Some scholars also compare Ahiqar, the wise counselor at an Assyrian court in Tobit and the Story of Ahiqar. Achior's speech (5:5–21) is the book's summary of Israel's history; its theology returns in Judith's own words (11:10).

a: No lie will come out of your servant's mouth
p: Judith uses nearly the same words to Holofernes in 11:5, when she is about to deceive him.
b: Achior promises "no lie will come out of your servant's mouth," and he keeps his word. Judith tells Holofernes, "I will not tell my lord a lie tonight" (11:5, ouk anangelō pseudos), and then tells him a story meant to destroy him, while leaning on Achior's true account (11:9–10). The two speeches are meant to be read together; on Judith's deception see 11:5.

a: This people are descendants of the Chaldeans
p: Achior begins where Genesis does: Abraham's family came from "Ur of the Chaldeans".
b: Terah's family "went out with them from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan" (Genesis 11:31; compare Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:7, "who brought him out from Ur of the Chaldeans"). Achior's summary (5:6–19) follows the Bible's story from Abraham to the return from exile, like the Levites' prayer in Nehemiah 9:6–37 and Joshua's farewell (Joshua 24:2–13). Its nearest New Testament relatives are Stephen's speech in Acts 7:2–53 and Paul's in Acts 13:16–41, both told to hearers who need to know who Israel is.
r: Genesis 11:28–31; Genesis 15:7; Nehemiah 9:6–37; Joshua 24:2–13; Acts 7:2–53; Acts 13:16–41; Psalm 105

a: because they did not want to follow the gods of their ancestors
t: Compared with the Bible: Abraham leaves the idols
p: Genesis does not say why Abraham's family left Ur. Achior says they refused their ancestors' gods. This goes beyond the Bible.
b:
Agrees: Joshua 24:2 says that Terah's family "lived on the far side of the River … and they served other gods." Goes beyond: Genesis never says that Abraham turned from those gods or was driven out for it; in Genesis 11:31 Terah leads the move and God calls Abram later (Genesis 12:1).

Achior's version is one of the earliest witnesses to a Jewish tradition that grew rich later: in Jubilees 12 Abram burns his father's house of idols, and in Genesis Rabbah 38:13 he smashes the idols in Terah's shop and is thrown into Nimrod's furnace. Catholic and Orthodox readers, who count Judith as Scripture, read the speech as a true summary in a Gentile's mouth; Protestant readers value it as early Jewish interpretation of Genesis.

a: the God of heaven
p: A title of God common after the exile, in Persian-era books such as Ezra, Nehemiah and Daniel.
b: Cyrus's decree speaks of "the LORD, the God of the heavens" (Ezra 1:2), and Nehemiah prays "before the God of the heavens" (Nehemiah 1:4; compare Daniel 2:18; Jonah 1:9). It was a title that Jews could use with foreigners. Achior uses it here, and Bethulia prays to the "Lord God of heaven" (6:19). The Vulgate stresses the point: they worshiped "one God of heaven."
orig: τῷ θεῷ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (tō theō tou ouranou)

a: So they were thrown out from before their gods
p: The Greek says "they threw them out", with no subject. It is a Hebrew way of saying "they were thrown out".
b: Hebrew often uses "they" with no stated subject in place of a passive. The Greek exebalon autous, "they cast them out," probably means the Chaldeans drove Abraham's family away because of their new faith. Then "they fled to Mesopotamia," that is, to Haran in the north (Genesis 11:31; the Vulgate names Haran here). Achior thus calls Israel's ancestors refugees for their faith.
orig: ἐξέβαλον αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ προσώπου τῶν θεῶν αὐτῶν (exebalon autous apo prosōpou tōn theōn autōn)

a: Then their God told them to leave the place where they were living and go to the land of Canaan
p: Achior's line sums up Genesis 12:1–5 and 13:2.
b: God says to Abram, "Go on your way, out of your land, away from your kin and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you" (Genesis 12:1), and Abram "was very heavy with wealth: livestock, silver and gold" (Genesis 13:2). Achior leaves out the promises, Isaac and Jacob, and Joseph: he tells a military man what matters to him, where these people came from and how their God protects them.

a: because a famine had covered the face of the land of Canaan
p: The famine and the growth in Egypt follow Genesis 47 and Exodus 1.
b: Jacob's sons tell Pharaoh, "We have come to stay in the land as foreigners. In Canaan the famine is heavy" (Genesis 47:4), and "the Israelites were fruitful and swarmed. They grew many and became very, very strong" (Exodus 1:7). The Vulgate adds that they were there "four hundred years," the figure of Genesis 15:13.

a: They outwitted them
p: The rare Greek verb is the one the Septuagint uses in Exodus 1:10, and Stephen repeats it in Acts 7:19.
b: Pharaoh says, "Come on, let us outsmart them" (Exodus 1:10), in the Septuagint katasophisōmetha. Achior uses the same verb, katesophisanto, and so does Stephen in Acts 7:19 ("he dealt craftily with our people"). Then "they turned their lives bitter with hard labor in clay and bricks" (Exodus 1:14). Sinaiticus reads "clay and brick" here too (see the variant). The plural "they outwitted them" moves from the king to the Egyptians.

a: he struck the land of Egypt with plagues that had no cure
p: Achior compresses Exodus 7–12 into a sentence: the cry, the plagues, the Egyptians driving them out.
b: Israel's cry rose up to God (Exodus 2:23, "The Israelites sighed from their labor and cried out"), God struck Egypt, and in the end "Egypt leaned hard on the people to hurry and send them out of the land" (Exodus 12:33). Achior's whole speech has the pattern of the book of Judges: oppression, a cry to God, rescue. It is the pattern Bethulia is living through.

a: God dried up the Red Sea before them
t: The Red Sea or the Sea of Reeds
p: The Greek says "the Red Sea", the Septuagint's name for the sea the Hebrew calls Yam Suf, "the Sea of Reeds".
b: Hebrew yam suf means "Sea of Reeds," and this site's Plain of the Hebrew books uses that name (Nehemiah 9:9, "you heard their cry at the Sea of Reeds"). The Septuagint calls it hē erythra thalassa, "the Red Sea," and since Judith survives in Greek, the Plain here says "the Red Sea." Exodus tells how "he turned the sea into dry ground" (Exodus 14:21). Achior gives the crossing one clause; the Vulgate expands it with the walls of water and the drowned army.

a: and he led them on the road to Sinai and Kadesh-barnea
t: Compared with the Bible: Sinai without the law
p: Achior passes Sinai without a word about the covenant, Moses or the law. The omission is striking.
b: Exodus 19–24 is the heart of the Torah: God makes Israel "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6) and gives the law. Achior mentions Sinai only as a stop on the road, names no Moses, and skips the forty years. Agrees with the Bible's outline, but selects: a foreign officer explains Israel's strength to a general, so he tells of land, wars and God's protection, and refers to the covenant only as "the way he had laid down for them" (5:18). The Vulgate adds the sweetened water and the manna (5:15 in its numbering).

a: all the people of Heshbon
p: The defeat of Sihon, king of Heshbon, was Israel's first victory east of the Jordan.
b: Numbers tells how "Israel took all these towns, and Israel settled in all the towns of the Amorites, in Heshbon and all its villages" (Numbers 21:25), for "Heshbon was the city of Sihon king of the Amorites" (Numbers 21:26). An Ammonite might have added that Israel was told not to touch Ammon's land: "I will not give you any of the Ammonites' land" (Deuteronomy 2:19). Achior leaves his own people out of the story.

a: the people of Shechem
p: Achior's list follows the lists in Joshua and adds Shechem, the town Simeon destroyed.
b: Joshua promises that God "will surely drive out ahead of you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites and the Jebusites" (Joshua 3:10). Achior adds "the people of Shechem." Genesis 34 tells how Simeon and Levi "each took his sword" and destroyed Shechem (Genesis 34:25). Uzziah (6:15) and Judith (9:2) are both of the tribe of Simeon, and Judith will pray to the God who gave Simeon that sword.

a: As long as they did not sin before their God, good things were theirs
p: Achior states Deuteronomy's teaching: Israel prospers when faithful and falls when it sins.
b:
This is the teaching of Deuteronomy 28 and of the books from Joshua to Kings: obedience brings blessing; turning away brings defeat and exile (Deuteronomy 28:25, 28:64; Judges 2:11–23). Scholars call this pattern Deuteronomistic.

The whole plot rests on it. Achior advises: find out whether they are sinning (5:20–21). Judith will use the same rule to trap Holofernes, telling him Israel is about to sin by eating forbidden food (11:10–15). Job and Ecclesiastes question whether life always follows the rule; Judith affirms it, but adds that God may test the faithful too (8:25–27).

a: the way he had laid down for them
p: The Greek verb is the one used for making a covenant.
b: The verb dietheto belongs with diathēkē, "covenant," and the Septuagint uses it for God's making a covenant (Genesis 15:18; Deuteronomy 5:2). "The way he covenanted for them" is Achior's word for the law that he never names.
orig: ὁδοῦ ἧς διέθετο αὐτοῖς (hodou hēs dietheto autois)

a: The temple of their God was razed to the ground
p: Achior speaks of the temple's destruction as past, to an officer of Nebuchadnezzar, the king who destroyed it.
b: Babylon's general "set the LORD's house on fire" (2 Kings 25:9) in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. Achior, serving a Nebuchadnezzar, tells it as old history. This is the same problem as 4:3: the book's "Nebuchadnezzar" rules after the exile. For readers who take the book as a parable, the effect is that every enemy of Israel, past and present, stands in one figure. "A land not their own" echoes God's words to Abram in Genesis 15:13.

a: They have come up from the Diaspora
p: Greek diaspora, "scattering", was the Septuagint's word for Israel scattered among the nations.
b: Deuteronomy's curse, "Every kingdom on earth will shudder at you" (Deuteronomy 28:25), is in the Septuagint "you will be in dispersion (en diaspora) in all the kingdoms." The word came to mean the Jewish communities outside the land (John 7:35; James 1:1; 1 Peter 1:1). Achior describes the return of Ezra 1–2, "let him go up to Jerusalem" (Ezra 1:3). "Because it was empty" repeats the view of 2 Chronicles 36:21 that the land lay desolate; archaeology shows that many people stayed.
r: Deuteronomy 28:25; Ezra 1:3; 2 Chronicles 36:21; John 7:35; James 1:1; 1 Peter 1:1

a: if there is any error in this people
p: Achior says: attack only if Israel is sinning. Balaam's advice to Moab was to make Israel sin.
b: Balaam could only say of Israel, "He sees no trouble in Jacob, / he finds no mischief in Israel" (Numbers 23:21). Later he advised Moab how to make Israel stumble (Numbers 31:16, "on Balaam's advice"; Revelation 2:14, Balaam "taught Balak to trap the Israelites"). Achior's "stumbling block" (skandalon) is Balaam's trap, seen from the other side: he tells the general not to attack unless God has already withdrawn his protection. Greek agnoēma means a sin of ignorance or error.

a: their Lord and their God will hold a shield over them
p: The verb is the one the Septuagint uses when God says to Abram, "I am a shield for you".
b: In the Greek of Genesis 15:1 God says "I am shielding you" (hyperaspizō); the site's Plain of the Hebrew has "I am a shield for you." Achior uses the same verb, and Holofernes throws it back at him (6:2). "We will be a disgrace before the whole earth" is the fear of every proud king in the Bible.

a: they are a people with no power and no strength for a hard battle
p: The officers are right, and that is the point: Israel's strength is not its army.
b: "These have chariots, and those have horses, / but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7). Judith's song will say the Lord is "a God who shatters wars" (16:2). The officers' scorn is true as far as it goes.

a: they will be a meal for your whole army
p: At the edge of Canaan, Joshua and Caleb said the enemy would be "our bread". Here the enemy says it of Israel.
b: Greek katabrōma, "food to be eaten," turns around Numbers 14:9: "do not be afraid of the people of the land, for they are our bread." In the wilderness story the spies' faith was right; the book invites the reader to expect the same reversal here.

a: the whole crowd of foreigners
p: Greek allophyloi, "other tribes", is the Septuagint's usual word for the Philistines.
b: In the Greek of Judges and Samuel allophyloi nearly always translates "Philistines." Here it means simply the many foreign peoples in Holofernes' army. The Plain renders it "foreigners." The Plain follows Alexandrinus in adding "and to all the Moabites" here (see the variants at 6:1 and 6:2).

a: you hirelings of Ephraim
p: Why Ephraim? Achior is an Ammonite. The phrase has puzzled every reader.
b: Ephraim was the chief tribe of northern Israel, and Holofernes elsewhere calls Achior "hireling of Ammon" (6:5). Some think "Ephraim" is an early copying error for "Ammon." Others take it as a sneer: Achior talks like a paid agent of the Israelites of the north, in whose hills Bethulia lies. A "hireling" (misthōtos) is a mercenary, which is what the Ammonites and Moabites are in Holofernes' eyes.

a: to play the prophet among us as you have today
p: Holofernes calls Achior a prophet to mock him. Like Balaam, the foreign prophet, Achior turns out to be right.
b: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, but "Would he say a thing and not do it?" (Numbers 23:19); Balaam could speak only what God gave him. Achior is no prophet by trade, but his words come true to the letter: Israel cannot be beaten unless it sins (5:20–21; 11:10), and Holofernes falls. Holofernes, who calls Achior's words "prophecy," will be killed by the people he despises (13:6–8).

a: Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?
p: The book's central question. Pharaoh, the Rabshakeh and Daniel's Nebuchadnezzar asked versions of it.
b:
Pharaoh: "Who is this LORD, that I should heed his voice by letting Israel go?" (Exodus 5:2). The Rabshakeh at Jerusalem: "Which one of all the gods of these lands has rescued his land from my hand? And the LORD is going to rescue Jerusalem from my hand?" (2 Kings 18:35). Daniel's Nebuchadnezzar asks the three young men what god could rescue them from his hands (Daniel 3:15). Each time the question is answered by God himself.

Israel's answer stands in the Song of Moses: "I, only I, am he; / there is no god alongside me" (Deuteronomy 32:39), and in Judith's prayer that all nations will know "that you are the God of all power and strength, and that no one but you shields the race of Israel" (9:14). The Greek tis ho theos, "who is the god," leaves no doubt that Holofernes means divinity, not just power (compare 3:8).

a: like one man
p: God promised Gideon he would strike Midian "as if it were one man". Holofernes borrows the promise.
b: God tells Gideon, "I will be with you. You will strike down Midian as if it were one man" (Judges 6:16). In Holofernes' mouth the words mean an easy, total slaughter. Readers who know Judges know who wins when those words are spoken. "The power of our horses" recalls Pharaoh's horses and chariots that sank in the sea (Exodus 15:1).

a: We will burn them up with them
p: The Greek is obscure: burn them with what, or among whom?
b: Greek katakausomen gar autous en autois, "we will burn them in/with them." It may be a Hebrew bam, "among them" or "with them," meaning their towns, or it may refer to the horses of 6:3. Sinaiticus leaves out "with them." The KJV has "with them we will tread them under foot." The Plain keeps the obscurity rather than guess.
orig: κατακαύσομεν γὰρ αὐτοὺς ἐν αὐτοῖς (katakausomen gar autous en autois)

a: Their land will be drunk with their blood
p: A picture from the prophets' oracles against Edom and Israel's enemies, here turned against Israel.
b: God says in the Song of Moses, "I will make my arrows drunk with blood" (Deuteronomy 32:42), and Isaiah sees Edom's land soaked with blood (Isaiah 34:5–7). Holofernes turns the image against God's people. The Greek horia, "borders, territory," is "mountains" in Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (see the variant).

a: the words he has said will not be empty
p: Holofernes ends with a claim the Bible makes for God's word alone.
b: "God is not a man, that he should lie … Would he speak and not carry it out?" (Numbers 23:19). Of Samuel it was said that the LORD let none of his words fall (1 Samuel 3:19), and in Isaiah God says his word will not come back to him empty (Isaiah 55:11). Holofernes says it of Nebuchadnezzar twice (6:4; 6:9). The book's answer comes when Holofernes' own head is cut off with his own sword (13:6–8).

a: this people that came out of Egypt
t: "The people who came out of Egypt"
p: Balak of Moab used the same words about Israel when he hired Balaam.
b: Balak sent for Balaam saying, "Look, a people has come out of Egypt. Look, they cover the face of the land" (Numbers 22:5). Holofernes sneers at the exodus that Achior has just told (5:12–13). The scene keeps echoing Numbers 22–24: a foreign power, Moabite advisers, a foreigner who can speak only truth about Israel.

a: the iron of my army
p: Iron stands for the sword. Holofernes promises Achior a sword through his sides.
b: The Greek sidēros, "iron," is used for a blade, as Hebrew barzel can be. The threat is ironic: it is Holofernes whose life will end by a sword, his own, in the hand of a woman (13:6–8). "When they come back" follows Vaticanus; correctors of Vaticanus and the other great codices read "when I come back" (see the variant).

a: You will not die until you are destroyed along with them
p: Holofernes' sentence turns into Achior's rescue: he will share Israel's fate, and Israel is saved.
b: Holofernes means to make Achior watch the destruction of the people he praised and then die with them. Like Haman's plans in Esther (Esther 7:10) the plan turns back on its maker. Achior is handed to Israel, welcomed (6:20–21), and later joins Israel for good (14:10). Placing him "in one of the towns on the passes" (6:7) is how the author gets the Ammonite into Bethulia.

a: do not let your face fall
p: A Hebrew idiom for looking downcast, the words God says to Cain.
b: God asks Cain, "Why are you burning with anger? Why has your face fallen?" (Genesis 4:6). Holofernes sneers: if you are so sure they will not be taken, why look so gloomy? The Greek mē sympesetō sou to prosōpon copies the Hebrew idiom.
orig: μὴ συμπεσέτω σου τὸ πρόσωπον (mē sympesetō sou to prosōpon)

a: the springs below Bethulia
p: Bethulia's water comes from springs at the foot of its hill. They are the key to the siege.
b: Hill towns in the land drew water from springs at the foot of their hill and stored rain in cisterns. Holofernes will seize the springs (7:7, 7:17), the cisterns will run dry (7:21), and later Judith will bathe at the spring in the camp each night (12:7). Hezekiah once stopped up the springs outside Jerusalem so that "Assyria's kings" would not find water (2 Chronicles 32:3–4); here the Assyrians take the water instead.

a: All the slingers kept them from coming up by hurling stones at them
p: Slingers were deadly in hill country. The tribe of Benjamin was famous for them.
b: A sling could throw a stone the size of an egg with great force; Benjamin had seven hundred men who "could hit a single hair with a slingstone, never missing" (Judges 20:16), and David killed Goliath with one (1 Samuel 17:49). The townsmen do not know that the men below have come to deliver a friend.

a: Uzziah son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon
p: This Uzziah is the ruler of Bethulia, not King Uzziah of Judah. Like Judith he is a Simeonite.
b: The name (Hebrew 'Uzziyyah, "my strength is the LORD") was borne by a famous king of Judah (2 Kings 15:1–7; 2 Chronicles 26), but this Uzziah is a town ruler. He is from Simeon, the tribe of Judith too (9:2), whose ancestor took the sword at Shechem (Genesis 34:25). Simeon's land was in the far south of Judah (Joshua 19:1–9), not in Samaria, another sign that the book's geography is symbolic.

a: Chabris son of Othniel, and Charmis son of Malchiel
t: Names from the days of the Judges
p: Othniel was Israel's first judge, and Malchiel and Carmi are old tribal names.
b: The Greek Gothoniēl is the Septuagint's spelling of Othniel, the first of the judges, whom "the LORD raised up" when Israel cried out (Judges 3:9). Malchiel is a grandson of Asher (Genesis 46:17), and Charmis may be the Carmi of Genesis 46:9. The names place Bethulia in the world of the Judges, the world of Deborah and Jael, which the book will echo again (Judges 4–5).
orig: Χαβρεὶς ὁ τοῦ Γοθονιὴλ καὶ Χαρμεὶς υἱὸς Μελχειήλ (Chabreis ho tou Gothoniēl kai Charmeis huios Melcheiēl)

a: the assembly
t: Compared with the Bible: an Ammonite in Israel's assembly
p: Achior stands in the middle of Israel's "assembly", the very assembly the Torah closes to Ammonites.
b:
The Greek ekklēsia is the Septuagint's word for Hebrew qahal, "assembly," as in "No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. Even to the tenth generation" (Deuteronomy 23:3). Nehemiah enforced it (Nehemiah 13:1, "no Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of God, ever").

Judith goes further than standing in the assembly: in 14:10 Achior is circumcised and "joined to the house of Israel," which conflicts with the letter of Deuteronomy 23:3. Later rabbis discussed whether that law still applied (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4). Christian readers who hold Judith as Scripture see in Achior a sign of the nations coming to Israel's God (Isaiah 56:3–7). See 14:10.

a: look today on the faces of those who are set apart for you
p: The short prayer asks God to look on his holy people, and on their humiliation.
b: "you are a people holy to the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 7:6); "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). The prayer's three verbs, look down, have pity, look on, set the pride of the enemy against the "low state" (tapeinōsis) of Israel, the word that ends the part at 7:32. Hannah asks God to look on the low state of his servant, and Mary sings that he has done so, both with the Greek word tapeinōsis (1 Samuel 1:11; Luke 1:48).

a: gave a banquet for the elders
t: A banquet and a night of prayer
p: The Greek word means a drinking party. It stands against Holofernes' banquets later.
b: Greek potos is a feast with wine. Uzziah's small feast for the elders, followed by a night of prayer, is a quiet counterpart to Holofernes' great drinking party, where he drinks himself senseless (12:10–20). The Vulgate says they ate "after their fast was over" and then prayed all night intra ecclesiam, "within the church" (Douay), meaning the place of assembly.

a: a hundred and seventy thousand foot soldiers
p: In 2:15 the army had 120,000 foot soldiers. By Bethulia it has 170,000, swollen by allies.
b: The extra fifty thousand are presumably the allies taken from the coastal towns (3:6) and the "mixed crowd" (2:20). The Vulgate gives 120,000 foot and 22,000 horse here. Swete's apparatus also reports a different number in Sinaiticus (see the variant).

a: Dothan
p: At Dothan an army once surrounded Elisha, and the hills were full of God's fiery chariots.
b: "All around the town stood an army, horses and chariots," and Elisha's servant cried out; then "the hill was filled with horses and fiery chariots, surrounding Elisha" (2 Kings 6:15–17). Bethulia is besieged by the same town, by a greater army. The first readers would recall that God's help can be present when no one sees it. Belbaim may be Ibleam (Joshua 17:11) and Cyamon perhaps Jokneam; neither is certain.

a: Now these men will lick clean the face of the whole land
t: Like an ox licking the grass
p: The words come from Moab's fear of Israel in Numbers 22:4, now in Israel's mouth.
b: Moab said of Israel, "Now this crowd will lick clean everything around us, the way an ox licks the green plants of the field bare" (Numbers 22:4). The Greek verb is the same (ekleichō). Israel now feels what Moab felt, and Moabites are among the enemy (7:8). Again the story runs through Numbers 22–24.

a: He seized them and set camps of soldiers over them
p: Rather than storm the heights, Holofernes takes the water.
b: Ancient sieges were often won by thirst and hunger rather than assault. Jerusalem's famine under Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:3) and the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:24–29) were remembered with horror. Holofernes' allies will spell out the plan (7:9–15): no battle, only waiting.

a: the descendants of Esau
p: Edom, Esau's people, joined Babylon against Jerusalem. The first readers knew Idumea as a rival nearby.
b: Psalm 137 remembers how Edom cheered as Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7), and Obadiah condemns Edom for joining Jerusalem's enemies. In the first readers' day Edom was Idumea, just south of Judea. Judas Maccabeus fought them (1 Maccabees 5:3, 5:65), and John Hyrcanus forced them to be circumcised and keep the Jewish law, in the late 100s BC; the date is debated (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258).

a: the heights of the mountains where they live
p: The Greek says "the mountains in which they live in them", copying a Hebrew relative clause.
b: Greek en hois autoi enoikousin en autois, "in which they dwell in them," repeats the pronoun the way Hebrew does after asher ("which"). Good Greek would not. Such small slips are among the strongest evidence that Judith was translated from Hebrew. The advisers' point is military: Israel trusts its hills, not its spears.
orig: ἐν οἷς αὐτοὶ ἐνοικοῦσιν ἐν αὐτοῖς (en hois autoi enoikousin en autois)

a: Thirst will kill them, and they will give up their town
t: Water and the testing of God
p: Thirst brought Israel to test God at Massah. The siege brings Bethulia to the same place.
b: At Rephidim "the people picked a fight with Moses. They said, 'Give us water so we can drink'" (Exodus 17:2), and there "they put the LORD on trial" (Exodus 17:7). Deuteronomy remembers it: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16). Bethulia's thirst will lead to the five-day limit (7:30) that Judith calls testing God (8:12).

a: So you will pay them back with an evil reward
p: The Greek repeats the same root, as Hebrew likes to do.
b: Greek antapodōseis autois antapodoma ponēron, "you will repay them an evil repayment," is a Hebrew cognate construction. In the Bible it is God who "repays" (Deuteronomy 32:35; Psalm 94:2). The crime, in the advisers' eyes, is that Israel did not come out to meet Holofernes "in peace," as the coast did (3:1–4).
orig: ἀνταποδώσεις αὐτοῖς ἀνταπόδομα πονηρὸν (antapodōseis autois antapodoma ponēron)

a: opposite Egrebel, which is near Chus on the wadi Mochmur
p: Egrebel is often identified with Aqraba, southeast of Shechem. Chus and the wadi Mochmur are unknown.
b: Commentators have identified Egrebel with the village of Aqraba (ancient Akrabeta), about eight miles southeast of Shechem. If that is right, the army spreads across the hills of Samaria from the Jezreel Valley to the south. Chus and the Mochmur ravine have not been securely identified.

a: for their spirit sank
p: Greek ōligopsychēsen, "became small-souled", is the word of Israel's despair in Egypt.
b: The Septuagint uses the noun of this verb (oligopsychia) in Exodus 6:9, where Israel would not listen to Moses "because their spirit was worn short and their labor was hard." The same weakness of spirit, under the same kind of pressure, will lead Bethulia to demand surrender (7:23–28).
orig: ὠλιγοψύχησεν τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῶν (ōligopsychēsen to pneuma autōn)

a: Their little children lost heart
p: The scene recalls the laments for Jerusalem's fall under Nebuchadnezzar.
b: Lamentations mourns infants fainting in the city squares and children asking their mothers for bread and wine (Lamentations 2:11–12; Lamentations 2:19; Lamentations 4:4). Bethulia faces the same fate. The book shows the suffering honestly; its answer comes in the next chapters.

a: May God judge between you and us!
t: "May God judge between you and us"
p: The words of Sarai to Abram and David to Saul: a bitter appeal to God against someone close.
b: Sarai said, "Let the LORD judge between me and you" (Genesis 16:5), and David said to Saul, "Let the LORD be judge between me and you" (1 Samuel 24:12). The people turn the formula on their own leaders. Their charge is that Uzziah should have made peace, as the coastal towns did (3:1–4).

a: You have done us a great wrong by not making peace with the Assyrians
t: Compared with the Bible: surrender or resist?
p: Jeremiah told Jerusalem to surrender to Nebuchadnezzar and live. Judith tells Israel to resist him.
b:
Under the real Nebuchadnezzar, Jeremiah said: whoever goes out and surrenders to the Babylonians will live (Jeremiah 21:9; Jeremiah 38:17–18), because God had handed Judah over for its sins. The people of Bethulia say much the same (7:26–27).

In Judith they are wrong, because Israel has not sinned (5:20–21; 8:18–20) and the war is about worship: to surrender is to accept Nebuchadnezzar as god (3:8). So the two books differ in situation, not in principle: both teach that the outcome depends on Israel's faithfulness. The first readers had lived through a war of faith, when the choice was to give up the law or fight (1 Maccabees 2:15–28).

a: God has sold us into their hands
p: The phrase of the book of Judges: God "sold" Israel to its enemies when it sinned.
b: "He sold them to the enemies around them" (Judges 2:14); "So the LORD sold them to Jabin king of Canaan" (Judges 4:2; compare Deuteronomy 32:30). The people read their suffering as punishment, as Judges would (7:28). Judith will answer that it may be a test, not a punishment (8:25–27).

a: It is better for us to become their plunder
p: The wilderness generation said the same: better to serve Egypt than to die.
b: "Serving Egypt is better for us than dying in the wilderness" (Exodus 14:12); "Our wives and our little ones will become plunder. Isn't going back to Egypt the better thing for us?" (Numbers 14:3). Bethulia's cry is the old murmuring of Israel under pressure. The narrator does not mock it: the fear for children is real.

a: We call heaven and earth to witness against you
p: The people use Moses' covenant witnesses against their own rulers.
b: Moses said, "I call the heavens and the earth as witnesses against you today" (Deuteronomy 4:26; compare Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 31:28). The people's God "punishes us for our sins and for the sins of our ancestors," as in the Ten Words: "I bring the fathers' guilt home to the children" (Exodus 20:5). The Greek of the last words is hard; see the next note.

a: May he not do to us today what we have described!
p: The Greek says "that he may not do according to these words today". What "words" are meant is unclear.
b: Vaticanus reads hina mē poiēsē kata ta rhēmata tauta, "so that he may not do according to these words today." The Plain takes it as a wish: may God not bring on us what we have just described, the death of our children. Others take "he" as Uzziah and read "so that you may do as we have said." Sinaiticus leaves out "not," giving "that he may do according to these words today" (see the variant).
orig: ἵνα μὴ ποιήσῃ κατὰ τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ σήμερον (hina mē poiēsē kata ta rhēmata tauta en tē hēmera tē sēmeron)

a: Let us endure five more days
p: Uzziah's five days buy time but set God a limit. Judith will call it testing God (8:11–17).
b:
Uzziah means well. He calms a desperate crowd, and his words are full of hope: the Greek future "will turn" (epistrepsei) is a confident statement, not a "perhaps." But the promise to surrender if God does not act in five days makes God's help a condition with a deadline. Judith rebukes the elders: "Now who are you, to put God to the test today?" (8:12), echoing "Do not put the LORD your God to the test" (Deuteronomy 6:16).

The elders of Jabesh-gilead struck a similar bargain: "Leave us alone for seven days … If no one rescues us, we will come out to you" (1 Samuel 11:3). There, as here, rescue came in time. The Latin Vulgate, which tells the scene differently, makes Uzziah less sure: Forsitan enim indignationem suam abscindet, "for perhaps he will cut off his anger" (Vulgate 7:24).

a: And there was great distress in the town
p: The part ends with Bethulia "in great humiliation", the word of the prayer in 6:19.
b: The Greek en tapeinōsei pollē, "in great lowness," uses the noun of 6:19, where the people asked God to "have pity on the low state of our people," and of 4:9, where they "humbled" themselves. In the Bible God lifts up the lowly (1 Samuel 2:7–8; Luke 1:52). The next chapter introduces the one through whom he will do it.
